messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 32-year-old South Asian man, had always been a diligent worker. As a housekeeper in a bustling hotel, he took pride in ensuring that every room was immaculate for guests. However, his life took a harrowing turn one night as he was returning home from work. He had just stepped off the bus when he was approached by two men in a dimly lit alley. They demanded his belongings, and in the chaos, one of them struck him in the stomach. The pain was excruciating, a visceral agony that seemed to echo in his body long after the incident. He gave them his wallet, trembling not just from fear but from the sheer unpredictability of the world around him. That night, as he lay awake, the memory of the attack became a relentless specter; each time it returned, he felt the same physical pain in his gut, as if the trauma was etched into his very being. 

In the weeks that followed, Arjun found himself haunted by vivid recollections of the attack. The details were so clear that he could almost relive the moment—the glint of the knife, the harsh words of his assailants, and the suffocating realization that he was utterly vulnerable. Yet, when he attempted to describe the event to his wife, words failed him. He would start to explain but would often falter, feeling as if he were trapped in a fog that obscured his ability to articulate the fear that had gripped him. This struggle left him feeling isolated, as though he were carrying a burden that he could not share with anyone.

As the days turned into weeks, Arjun's perception of the world shifted dramatically. His belief that people were not what they seemed made the memories of the attack surge even more vividly; he began to think that these recollections were proof of the world’s inherent danger, reinforcing his negative view of those around him. He began to believe that people were not what they seemed; the kindness he had always experienced felt like a facade. The world outside his home now felt menacing, a dangerous place where anyone could turn into a threat. He started to avoid the alley where the mugging had occurred, taking longer routes to and from work, all the while feeling a knot of mistrust tighten within him. This wariness seeped into his relationships. Once open and friendly, he now found it difficult to engage with colleagues, convinced that they could not be trusted. Even small interactions felt fraught with danger, as though every person he encountered could harbor ill intentions.

Arjun's negative appraisals of people and the world around him began to reinforce his intrusive memories. The more he believed that he could not trust anyone, the more the memories of the attack plagued him. Each time the vivid recollection flashed back into his mind, it left him feeling even more convinced that he was weak and vulnerable, leading him to believe that he would forever be at the mercy of others. Whenever he felt the familiar knot of mistrust, memories of the mugging surged forth, reminding him of his vulnerability. He felt trapped in a cycle where his thoughts painted the world as an unsafe place, and those thoughts brought back the vivid memories of pain and helplessness. Each time he recalled the event, he would feel that same gut-wrenching pain, a physical manifestation of his emotional turmoil, leaving him feeling even more vulnerable and distrustful.

Despite his efforts to regain a sense of normalcy, Arjun struggled to cope. He began withdrawing from social gatherings, fearing that he might encounter someone who reminded him of his attackers. His relationship with his wife began to feel strained; she didn’t understand why he had become so distant, and he couldn’t find the words to explain. Arjun felt increasingly isolated, as if he were living in a bubble of mistrust and fear that distanced him from those he loved. 

Finally, after months of suffering and feeling trapped in his own mind, Arjun decided to seek help. Sitting in the therapist’s office, he felt a mix of fear and hope. He was terrified that he might never feel safe again, that the world would always remain a perilous place. Yet, deep down, he longed for the ability to trust again—to share his life with his wife without the weight of his trauma pulling him down. Arjun hoped that, through this process, he could find a way to reclaim the life that had once been so vibrant, before the darkness of the mugging had seeped into every corner of his existence.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey how negative appraisals influence or reinforce the memories of the traumatic event.
The vignette does not convey how the memories of the traumatic event influence or drive negative appraisals of the world.
